But when he writes that this honor was offered to Leo in the Council of Chalcedon (book 4, letters 76, 80; book 7, letter 76), he says what has no appearance of truth; nothing of the kind is found in the acts of that council. And Leo himself, who in many letters attacks the decree that was then made in honor of the See of Constantinople, would undoubtedly not have left out this argument, the most plausible of all, if it were true that he himself had refused what was given to him. A man who in other respects was rather too eager for honor would not have passed over what would have been to his praise. Gregory, therefore, is mistaken in saying that this title was conferred on the Roman See by the Council of Chalcedon; not to mention how absurd it is for him to say that it came from that sacred council, and yet to call it wicked, profane, abominable, proud, and blasphemous, indeed devised by the devil and proclaimed by the herald of Antichrist. And yet he adds that his predecessor refused it, lest by what was given to one individually, all priests should be deprived of their due honor. In another place he says, "No one ever wished to be called by such a name; no one claimed this rash name for himself, lest by seizing the honor of supremacy in the office of the pontificate, he might seem to deny it to all his brethren" (Gregory, book 4, letter 82).

I come now to jurisdiction, which the Roman Pontiff asserts, as an indisputable proposition, that he possesses over all churches. I am aware of the great disputes that existed on this subject in ancient times, for there never was a time when the Roman See did not aim at authority over other churches. And here it will not be out of place to investigate the means by which she gradually gained some influence. I am not now referring to that unlimited power which she seized at a comparatively recent period; the consideration of that we will postpone to its proper place. But it is worthwhile here to show briefly in what way, and by what means, she formerly raised herself so as to claim some authority over other churches. When the churches of the East were troubled and torn by the factions of the Arians under the Emperors Constantius and Constans, sons of Constantine the Great, and Athanasius, the chief defender of the orthodox faith, had been driven from his see, that calamity compelled him to come to Rome, so that by the authority of this see he might both restrain the rage of his enemies and strengthen the orthodox in their distress. He was received with honor by Julius, who was then bishop, and he persuaded the bishops of the West to undertake the defense of his cause. Therefore, when the orthodox stood in great need of outside help, and saw that their chief protection lay in the Roman See, they willingly bestowed on it all the authority they could. But the utmost extent of this was that its communion was held in high esteem, and it was considered a disgrace to be excommunicated by it. Dishonest and wicked men afterward added much to its authority, for when they wished to escape lawful tribunals, they fled to Rome as to a sanctuary. Accordingly, if any presbyter was condemned by his bishop, or if any bishop was condemned by the synod of his province, he appealed to Rome. These appeals the Roman bishops received more eagerly than they should have, because it seemed a kind of extraordinary power to intervene in matters with which their connection was so very remote. Thus, when Eutyches was condemned by Flavianus, Bishop of Constantinople, he complained to Leo that the sentence was unjust. Leo, nothing loath, no less presumptuously than hastily, took up the patronage of a bad cause, and inveighed bitterly against Flavianus as having condemned an innocent man without due investigation. And so the effect of Leo's ambition was that for a time the impiety of Eutyches was confirmed. It is certain that in Africa the same thing happened repeatedly. For whenever some scoundrel had been condemned by his ordinary judge, he fled to Rome and brought many slanderous charges against his own people. The Roman See was always ready to intervene. This dishonesty compelled the African bishops to decree that no one should carry an appeal beyond the sea, under pain of excommunication.

Be that as it may, let us consider what right or authority the Roman See possessed at that time. Ecclesiastical power may be reduced to four heads: namely, the ordination of bishops, the calling of councils, the hearing of appeals (or jurisdiction), and the infliction of admonitory chastisements or censures. All the ancient councils require that bishops be ordained by their own metropolitans; nowhere do they require application to the Roman Bishop, except within his own patriarchate. Gradually, however, it became customary for all Italian bishops to go to Rome for consecration, with the exception of the metropolitans, who did not allow themselves to be brought into such subjection. But when any metropolitan was to be ordained, the Roman Bishop sent one of his presbyters merely to be present, not to preside. An example of this kind survives in Gregory (book 2, letters 68, 70), in the consecration of Constantius of Milan after the death of Laurence. I do not, however, think that this was a very ancient custom. At first, as a mark of respect and goodwill, they sent deputies to one another to witness the ordination and to attest their communion. What was thus voluntary afterward began to be regarded as necessary. However that may be, it is certain that in ancient times the Roman Bishop had no power of ordaining except within the bounds of his own patriarchate, that is, as a canon of the Council of Nicaea expresses it, in the suburban churches. To ordination was added the sending of a synodical letter, but this implied no authority. The patriarchs were accustomed, immediately after their consecration, to attest their faith in a formal document, in which they declared that they assented to the sacred and orthodox councils. Thus, by giving an account of their faith, they mutually approved one another. If the Roman Bishop had received this confession from others and not given it himself, he would thereby have been acknowledged as superior. But since he was bound to give as well as to receive, and to be subject to the common law, this was a sign of equality, not of lordship. Of this we have an example in a letter of Gregory to Anastasius and Cyriac of Constantinople, and in another letter to all the patriarchs together (Gregory, book 1, letters 24, 25; book 6, letter 169).

Next come admonitions or censures. These the Roman bishops in ancient times both administered to others and received in their turn. Irenaeus sharply rebuked Victor for rashly troubling the Church with a ruinous schism over a matter of no importance. Victor submitted without objection. Holy bishops at that time were accustomed to use the freedom of brothers in admonishing and rebuking the Roman prelate when he happened to err. He in his turn, when the case required it, reminded others of their duty and reproved them for their faults. For when Cyprian urges Stephen to admonish the bishops of France, he does not ground this on Stephen's greater power, but on the common right that priests have with regard to one another (Cyprian, book 3, letter 13). I ask: if Stephen had then presided over France, would not Cyprian have said, "Restrain them, for they are yours"? But his language is very different: "The brotherly fellowship that binds us together requires that we admonish one another" (Cyprian, To Pompeius, Against the Letter of Stephen). And we see also with what severity of language this man, otherwise of a mild temper, inveighs against Stephen himself when he thinks him guilty of insolence. Therefore it does not yet appear in this respect that the Roman Bishop possessed any jurisdiction over those who did not belong to his province.

As to the calling of councils, it was the duty of every metropolitan to assemble a provincial synod at stated times. Here the Roman Bishop had no jurisdiction, while the Emperor alone could summon a general council. Had any of the bishops attempted this, not only would those outside the province not have obeyed the summons, but an uproar would immediately have arisen. Therefore the Emperor gave notice to all alike to attend. Socrates, indeed, relates that Julius remonstrated with the Eastern bishops for not having called him to the Council of Antioch, since it was forbidden by the canons that anything should be decided without the knowledge of the Roman Bishop (Tripartite History, book 4). But who does not see that this is to be understood of those decrees which bind the whole Church? At the same time, it is not strange if, out of deference both to the antiquity and size of the city and to the dignity of the see, no universal decree concerning religion should be made in the absence of the Bishop of Rome, provided he did not refuse to be present. But what has this to do with dominion over the whole Church? For we do not deny that he was one of the principal bishops, though we refuse to admit what the Romanists now contend for, namely, that he had power over all.

The fourth and remaining kind of power is that of hearing appeals. It is evident that supreme power belongs to him to whose tribunal appeals are made. Many had repeatedly appealed to the Roman Pontiff. He too had tried to bring cases under his own hearing, but he was always ridiculed whenever he went beyond his own boundaries. I say nothing of the East and of Greece; but it is certain that the bishops of France stoutly resisted when he seemed to assume authority over them. In Africa the matter was long disputed. For in the Council of Milevita, at which Augustine was present, when those who carried appeals beyond the sea were excommunicated, the Roman Pontiff tried to obtain an alteration of the decree, and sent legates to show that the privilege of hearing appeals had been given him by the Council of Nicaea. The legates produced acts of the council drawn from the armory of their own church. The African bishops resisted, and maintained that the Bishop of Rome was not to be believed in his own cause; accordingly, they said that they would send to Constantinople and other cities of Greece, where less suspect copies might be had. It was found that nothing like what the Romanists had alleged was contained in the acts, and so the decree which abolished the supreme jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff was confirmed. In this matter the outrageous effrontery of the Roman Pontiff was laid bare. For when he had fraudulently substituted the Council of Sardis for that of Nicaea, he was disgracefully caught in an obvious falsehood. But still greater and more shameless was the wickedness of those who added a fictitious letter to the council, in which some Bishop of Carthage condemns the arrogance of Aurelius, his predecessor, in daring to withdraw himself from obedience to the Apostolic See, and, surrendering himself and his church, humbly begs for pardon. These are the noble records of antiquity on which the majesty of the Roman See is founded, while under the pretext of antiquity they deal in falsehoods so childish that even a blind man could feel them. "Aurelius," he says, "puffed up with diabolical audacity and defiance, was rebellious against Christ and Saint Peter, and therefore deserved to be anathematized." What does Augustine say? And what of the many Fathers who were present at the Council of Milevita? But what need is there for a lengthy refutation of that absurd document, which not even the Romanists, if they have any modesty left, can look at without a deep sense of shame? So Gratian, whether through malice or ignorance I do not know, after quoting the decree that those who carry appeals beyond the sea are to be deprived of communion, adds the exception, "Unless perhaps they have appealed to the Roman See" (Gratian, part 2, question 4, chapter Placuit). What can you make of creatures like these, who are so devoid of common sense that they set down as an exception to the law the very thing on account of which, as everyone sees, the law was made? For the council, in condemning appeals beyond the sea, simply forbids an appeal to Rome. Yet this worthy expounder exempts Rome from the common law.

But (to settle the question at once) a single narrative will make plain what kind of jurisdiction belonged to the Roman Bishop. Donatus of Casa Nigra had accused Cecilianus, the Bishop of Carthage. Cecilianus was condemned without a hearing, for, having learned that the bishops had conspired against him, he refused to appear. The case was brought before the Emperor Constantine, who, wishing the matter to be ended by an ecclesiastical decision, committed the hearing of it to Melciades, the Roman Bishop, appointing as his colleagues some bishops from Italy, France, and Spain. If it was part of the ordinary jurisdiction of the Roman See to hear appeals in ecclesiastical cases, why did he allow others to be joined with him at the Emperor's discretion? Indeed, why does he undertake to decide by the command of the Emperor rather than by his own office? But let us hear what happened afterward (see Augustine, Letter 162, and elsewhere). Cecilianus prevails. Donatus of Casa Nigra is defeated in his slanderous action, and appeals. Constantine refers the decision of the appeal to the Bishop of Arles, who sits as judge to give sentence after the Roman Pontiff. French: "Voila l'Archeveque d'Arles assis pour retracter; si bon lui semble la sentence de l'Eveque Romain. au moins pour juger par dessus lui." Here is the Archbishop of Arles seated to overturn, if he thinks fit, the sentence of the Bishop of Rome, or at least to judge as his superior.

I know how many letters there are, how many rescripts and edicts, in which there is nothing that the pontiffs do not ascribe and confidently claim for themselves. But all men of the least understanding and learning know that most of them are in themselves so absurd that it is easy at first sight to detect the forge from which they came. Does any man of sense and sobriety think that Anacletus is the author of that famous interpretation given in Gratian under the name of Anacletus, namely, that Cephas means head? (Distinction 22, chapter Sacrosancta.) Numerous follies of the same kind, which Gratian has heaped together without judgment, the Romanists of the present day use against us in defense of their see. The smoke with which, in the former days of ignorance, they deceived the ignorant, they would still peddle in the present light. I am unwilling to take much trouble refuting things which, by their extreme absurdity, plainly refute themselves. I admit that there are genuine letters of ancient pontiffs in which they pronounce magnificent praises of the extent of their see. Such are some of the letters of Leo. For as he possessed learning and eloquence, so he was excessively eager for glory and dominion. But the real question is whether or not, when he extolled himself in this way, the churches believed his testimony. It appears that many were offended by his ambition, and also resisted his greed. In one place he appoints the Bishop of Thessalonica his vicar throughout Greece and other neighboring regions (Leo, Letter 85), and elsewhere gives the same office to the Bishop of Arles, or some other, throughout France (Letter 83). In the same way, he appointed Hormisdas, Bishop of Hispala, his vicar throughout Spain. But he consistently makes this reservation, that in giving such commissions the ancient privileges of the metropolitans were to remain safe and intact. These appointments, therefore, were made on the condition that no bishop should be hindered in his ordinary jurisdiction, no metropolitan in hearing appeals, no provincial council in ordering churches. But what else was this than to decline all jurisdiction, and to intervene only for the purpose of settling discord, so far as the law and nature of ecclesiastical communion allow?

In the time of Gregory that ancient rule was greatly changed. For when the empire was shaken and torn; when France and Spain were suffering from the many disasters they received again and again; when Illyricum was laid waste, Italy harassed, and Africa almost destroyed by unbroken calamities; then, in order that amid these civil upheavals the integrity of the faith might remain, or at least not entirely perish, the bishops in every quarter attached themselves more closely to the Roman Pontiff. In this way not only the dignity but also the power of the see increased enormously, although I attach no great importance to the means by which this was accomplished. It is certain that it was then greater than in former ages. And yet it was very different from the unbridled dominion of one man ruling others as he pleased. Still, the reverence paid to the Roman See was such that by its authority it could guide and restrain those whom their own colleagues were unable to keep to their duty. For Gregory is careful again and again to testify that he was no less faithful in preserving the rights of others than in insisting that his own be preserved. "I do not," he says, "under the spur of ambition, detract from any man's right, but desire to honor my brethren in all things" (Gregory, book 2, letter 68). There is no sentence in his writings in which he boasts more proudly of the extent of his primacy than the following: "I do not know what bishop is not subject to the Roman See when he is found in a fault" (Leo, book 2, letter 68). However, he immediately adds, "Where faults do not call for intervention, all are equal according to the rule of humility." He claims for himself the right of correcting those who have sinned; if all do their duty, he puts himself on a footing of equality. He did indeed claim this right, and those who chose agreed to it, while those who were not pleased with it were free to object with impunity; and it is known that most of them did so. We may add that he is there speaking of the primate of Byzantium, who, when condemned by a provincial synod, rejected the whole judgment. His colleagues had informed the Emperor of his defiance, and the Emperor had committed the hearing of the matter to Gregory. We see, therefore, that he does not interfere in any way with the ordinary jurisdiction, and that in acting as an auxiliary to others he acts entirely by the Emperor's command.

At this time, therefore, the whole power of the Roman Bishop consisted in opposing stubborn and unruly spirits where some extraordinary remedy was required, and this in order to assist other bishops, not to interfere with them. Accordingly, he assumes no more power over others than he elsewhere grants others over himself, when he confesses that he is ready to be corrected by all and amended by all (book 2, letter 37). So in another place, though he orders the Bishop of Aquileia to come to Rome to plead his cause in a doctrinal controversy that had arisen between himself and others, he gives this order not by his own authority but in obedience to the Emperor's command. Nor does he declare that he himself will be the sole judge, but promises to call a synod by which the whole matter may be decided. But although moderation still prevailed to the extent that the power of the Roman See had certain limits it was not permitted to overstep, and the Roman Bishop himself was no more above others than under them, it is evident how dissatisfied Gregory was with this state of affairs. For he complains again and again that under the guise of the episcopate he had been brought back into the world, and was more entangled in earthly cares than when he lived as a layman; that in that honorable office he was oppressed by the tumult of secular affairs. Elsewhere he says, "So many burdensome occupations weigh me down that my mind cannot rise at all to the things above. I am tossed by the many billows of business, and after they are calmed I am afflicted by the storms of a tumultuous life, so that I may truly say, I have come into the depths of the sea, and the flood has overwhelmed me." From this I infer what he would have said if he had fallen on the present times. If he did not fully discharge the duty of a pastor, he at least did it. He declined the administration of civil power, and acknowledged himself subject, like others, to the Emperor. He did not interfere in the management of other churches unless forced by necessity. And yet he thinks himself in a labyrinth, because he cannot devote himself entirely to the duty of a bishop.

At that time, as has already been said, the Bishop of Constantinople was disputing the primacy with the Bishop of Rome. For after the seat of empire was fixed at Constantinople, the majesty of the empire seemed to require that its church should have the next place of honor after that of Rome. And certainly, at the outset, nothing had done more to give the primacy to Rome than the fact that it was then the capital of the empire. In Gratian (Distinction 80) there is a rescript under the name of Pope Lucinus, to the effect that the only way in which the cities where metropolitans and primates ought to preside were distinguished was by the civil government that had previously existed. There is a similar rescript under the name of Pope Clement, in which he says that patriarchs were appointed in those cities which had previously had the chief flamens. Although this is absurd, it was borrowed from something true. For it is certain that, in order to make as little change as possible, provinces were distributed according to the existing state of affairs, and primates and metropolitans were placed in those cities which surpassed others in honors and power. Accordingly, it was decreed in the Council of Turin that the cities of every province which were first in civil government should be the first sees of bishops. But if it should happen that the honor of civil government was transferred from one city to another, then the right of the metropolis should at the same time be transferred there. But Innocent, the Roman Pontiff, seeing that the ancient dignity of the city had been declining ever since the seat of empire was moved to Constantinople, and fearing for his see, enacted a contrary law, in which he denies that metropolitan churches must be changed as the imperial metropolitan cities were changed. But the authority of a synod is rightly to be preferred to the opinion of one individual, and Innocent himself should be suspect in his own cause. However that may be, by his very caveat he shows that the original rule was that metropolitans should be distributed according to the order of the empire.

In keeping with this ancient custom, the first Council of Constantinople decreed that the bishop of that city should take precedence after the Roman Pontiff, because it was a new Rome. But long afterward, when a similar decree was made at Chalcedon, Leo protested sharply (Socrates, Hist. Trop., book 9, chapter 13). And not only did he allow himself to set at nothing what six hundred bishops or more had decreed, but he even attacked them with bitter reproaches, because they had detracted from other sees in the honor which they had presumed to confer on the Church of Constantinople (in the Decretum, Distinction 22, chapter Constantinop.). What, I ask, could have moved the man to trouble the world over so small a matter but sheer ambition? He says that what the Council of Nicaea had once sanctioned ought to have been inviolable; as if the Christian faith were in any danger if one church was preferred to another, or as if separate patriarchates had been established on any other ground than that of civil order. But we know that civil order varies with the times, and indeed requires various changes. It is therefore futile for Leo to claim that the See of Constantinople ought not to receive the honor which was given to that of Alexandria by the authority of the Council of Nicaea. For common sense dictates that the decree was one of those which might be repealed in view of a change of times. What shall we say of the fact that none of the Eastern churches, though they were chiefly concerned, objected? Proterius, who had been appointed at Alexandria in place of Dioscorus, was certainly present; other patriarchs whose honor was diminished were present. It belonged to them to intervene, not to Leo, whose standing remained intact. When all of them are silent, many assent, and the Roman Bishop alone resists, it is easy to judge what moves him: namely, that he foresaw what happened not long afterward, that when the glory of ancient Rome declined, Constantinople, not content with the second place, would dispute the primacy with her. And yet his outcry was not so successful as to prevent the decree of the council from being ratified. Accordingly, his successors, seeing themselves defeated, quietly abandoned that petulance, and allowed the Bishop of Constantinople to be regarded as the second patriarch.

But shortly afterward John, who in the time of Gregory presided over the church of Constantinople, went so far as to call himself universal patriarch. Here Gregory, so as not to fail his see in a most excellent cause, steadily opposed him. And certainly it was impossible to tolerate the pride and madness of John, who wished to make the limits of his bishopric equal to the limits of the empire. What Gregory denies to another he does not claim for himself, but abhors the title, by whomever it is used, as wicked, impious, and abominable. Indeed, he is offended with Eulogius, Bishop of Alexandria, who had honored him with this title. "See," he says (book 8, letter 30), "in the address of the letter you have sent me, though I forbade it, you have taken care to write a word of proud meaning by calling me Universal Pope. What I ask is that your holiness go no further, because whatever is given to another beyond what reason requires is taken away from you. I do not count that as honor by which I see the honor of my brethren diminished. For my honor is the honor of the universal Church, and the full prerogative of my brethren. If your holiness calls me universal Pope, it denies itself to be that whole which it acknowledges me to be." The cause of Gregory was indeed good and honorable; but John, aided by the favor of the Emperor Maurice, could not be turned from his purpose. Cyriac also, his successor, never allowed himself to be spoken to on the subject.

At length Phocas, who had slain Maurice and usurped his place (and who was more friendly to the Romans, for what reason I do not know, or rather because he had been crowned king there without opposition), granted to Boniface III what Gregory had by no means demanded, namely, that Rome should be the head of all the churches. In this way the controversy was ended. And yet this kindness of the Emperor to the Romans would not have been of very much use had not other circumstances arisen. For shortly afterward Greece and all Asia were cut off from his communion, while all the reverence he received from France was obedience only so far as she pleased. She was first brought into subjection when Pepin gained possession of the throne. For Zachary, the Roman Pontiff, having aided him in his treachery and robbery when he expelled the lawful sovereign and seized the kingdom, which lay exposed as a kind of prey, was rewarded by having the jurisdiction of the Roman See established over the churches of France. Just as robbers are accustomed to divide and share the common spoil, those two worthies arranged that Pepin should have the worldly and civil power by plundering the true prince, while Zachary should become the head of all the bishops and have the spiritual power. This, though weak at first (as usually happens with new power), was afterward confirmed by the authority of Charlemagne for a very similar reason. For he too was under obligation to the Roman Pontiff, to whose zeal he owed the honor of empire. Though there is reason to believe that the churches had already been greatly altered before this, it is certain that only then was the ancient form of the Church completely effaced in Gaul and Germany. There are still extant, among the archives of the Parliament of Paris, brief chronicles of those times which, in treating of ecclesiastical affairs, mention the compacts of both Pepin and Charlemagne with the Roman Pontiff. From this we may infer that the ancient state of affairs was changed at that time.

From that time on, while matters everywhere were growing daily worse, the tyranny of the Roman Bishop was established and continually increased, and this partly through the ignorance and partly through the sluggishness of the bishops. For while he was claiming everything for himself, and going further and further in exalting himself beyond measure, contrary to law and right, the bishops did not exert themselves as zealously as they ought in curbing his pretensions. And even if they had not been lacking in spirit, they were devoid of true doctrine and experience, so that they were by no means fit for so important an effort. Accordingly, we see how great and monstrous was the profanation of all sacred things, and the dissolution of the whole ecclesiastical order, at Rome in the age of Bernard. He complains (On Consideration, to Eugenius, book 1) that the ambitious, the greedy, the demon-possessed, the sacrilegious, fornicators, the incestuous, and similar scoundrels flocked from every part of the world to Rome, so that by apostolic authority they might obtain or keep ecclesiastical honors; and that fraud, deceit, and violence prevailed. The manner of judging cases then in use he describes as detestable, and as a disgrace not only to the Church but to the courts. He exclaims that the Church is filled with the ambitious, and that no one is more afraid to commit crimes than robbers in their den when they share the spoils of the traveler. "Few," he says, "look to the mouth of the lawgiver, but all to his hands. Not without reason, however, for their hands do all the business of the Pope. What kind of thing is it when those who say to you, Well done, well done, are bought with the spoils of the Church? The life of the poor is sown in the highways of the rich; silver glitters in the mire; they run together from all sides; it is not the poorer man who picks it up, but the stronger, or perhaps the one who runs fastest. That custom, however, or rather that death, did not begin with you; I wish it would end with you. While these things are going on, you, a pastor, come forth robed in much costly clothing. If I may presume to say it, this is more the pasture of demons than of sheep. Peter, no doubt, acted this way; Paul amused himself this way. Your court has been more accustomed to receive good men than to make them. The bad do not gain much there, but the good degenerate." Then, when he describes the abuses of appeals, no godly man can read his account without horror. At length, speaking of the unbridled greed of the Roman See in usurping jurisdiction, he concludes thus (book 3, On Consideration): "I express the murmuring and common complaint of the churches. Their cry is that they are maimed and dismembered. There are none, or very few, who do not lament or fear that plague. Do you ask what plague? Abbots are encroached upon by bishops, bishops by archbishops, and so on. It would be strange if this could be excused. By acting this way you prove that you have the fullness of power, but not the fullness of righteousness. You do this because you are able; but whether you also ought to do it is the question. You are appointed to preserve, not to begrudge, the honor and rank of each." I have thought it proper to quote these few passages out of many, partly so that my readers may see how grievously the Church had then fallen, and partly so that they may see with what grief and lamentation all godly men beheld this calamity.

But even if we were to concede to the Roman Pontiff of the present day the eminence and extent of jurisdiction which his see had in the middle ages, as in the time of Leo and Gregory, what would that have to do with the existing Papacy? I am not now speaking of worldly dominion or civil power, which will be explained later in their own place (chapter 11, sections 8-14); but what resemblance is there between the spiritual government of which they boast and the state of those times? The only definition they give of the Pope is that he is the supreme head of the Church on earth, and the universal bishop of the whole world. The pontiffs themselves, when they speak of their authority, declare with great haughtiness that the power of commanding belongs to them; that the duty of obedience rests with others; that all their decrees are to be regarded as confirmed by the divine voice of Peter; that provincial synods, lacking the presence of the Pope, are deficient in authority; that they can ordain the clergy of any church; and that they can summon to their see any who have been ordained elsewhere. Countless things of this kind are contained in the hodgepodge of Gratian, which I do not mention, so as not to weary my readers. The whole comes to this: that to the Roman Pontiff belongs the supreme hearing of all ecclesiastical cases, whether in determining and defining doctrines, or in enacting laws, or in appointing discipline, or in pronouncing sentences. It would also be tedious and superfluous to review the privileges which they assume for themselves in what they call reservations. But the most intolerable thing of all is that they leave no judicial authority in the world to restrain and curb them when they licentiously abuse their immense power. "No man," they say (Nicolas, whose view is given in the Decretum, 17, question 3, chapter Nemini; Innocent IX, question 3, chapter Nemo; Symmachus, 9, question 3, chapter Aliorum; Antherius, in the same place, chapter Facta.

And so that edicts of this kind might carry more weight, they falsely inserted the names of ancient pontiffs, as if matters had been so arranged from the beginning, while it is absolutely certain that whatever attributes more to the Pontiff than we have shown was given to him by the ancient councils is new and of recent invention. Indeed, they have carried their effrontery so far as to publish a rescript under the name of Anastasius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, in which he testifies that it was laid down by ancient regulations that nothing should be done in the remotest provinces without first being referred to the Roman See. Besides its extreme folly, who can believe that such a eulogy of the Roman See came from an opponent and rival of its honor and dignity? But no doubt it was necessary that those Antichrists should proceed to such a degree of madness and blindness that their wickedness might be manifest to all men of sound mind who will only open their eyes. The decretal letters collected by Gregory IX, and also the Clementines and the Extravagants of Martin, breathe this still more plainly, and in more bombastic terms proclaim this boundless ferocity and tyranny, as it were, of barbarian kings. But these are the oracles by which the Romanists would have their Papacy judged. From these have sprung those famous axioms which have the force of oracles throughout the Papacy at the present day: namely, that the Pope cannot err; that the Pope is superior to councils; that the Pope is the universal bishop of all churches and the chief Head of the Church on earth. I say nothing of the still greater absurdities babbled by the foolish canonists in their schools, absurdities which, however, the Roman theologians not only assent to but even applaud, in flattery of their idol.

I will not deal with them on the strictest terms. Against their great insolence, some would quote the words which Cyprian addressed to the bishops in the council over which he presided: "None of us styles himself bishop of bishops, or forces his colleagues into the necessity of obeying by the tyranny of terror." Some might cite what was decreed long afterward at Carthage, "Let no one be called the prince of priests or first bishop," and might gather many proofs from history, canons from councils, and many passages from ancient writers, which bring the Roman Pontiff into his due order. But these I pass over, so as not to seem to press too hard upon them. However, let these worthy defenders of the Roman See tell me with what face they can defend the title of universal bishop, when they see it so often anathematized by Gregory. If his testimony is to stand, then by making their Pontiff universal they declare him to be Antichrist. The name of head was no more approved. For Gregory speaks thus: "Peter was the chief member in the body; John, Andrew, and James were the heads of particular communities. All, however, are members of the Church under one head. Indeed, the saints before the law, the saints under the law, the saints under grace, all completing the body of the Lord, are constituted members; none of them ever wished to be called universal" (Gregory, book 4, letter 83). When the Pontiff claims for himself the power of commanding, he agrees poorly with what Gregory says elsewhere. For when Eulogius, Bishop of Alexandria, said that he had received an order from him, he replies in this way: "This word order I beg you to remove from my hearing, for I know who I am and who you are: in station you are my brethren, in character my fathers. I therefore did not order, but took care to suggest what seemed useful" (Gregory, book 7, letter 80). When the Pope extends his jurisdiction without limit, he does great and outrageous injustice not only to other bishops but to every single church, tearing and dismembering them so that he may build his see on their ruins. When he exempts himself from all tribunals, and wishes to reign like a tyrant, holding his own whim to be his only law, the thing is too insulting, and too foreign to ecclesiastical order, to be submitted to on any account. It is utterly abhorrent not only to godly feeling but also to common sense.

But so that I may not be forced to discuss and pursue each point one by one, I again appeal to those who today would be thought the best and most faithful defenders of the Roman See: are they not ashamed to defend the existing state of the Papacy, which is plainly a hundred times more corrupt than in the days of Gregory and Bernard, though even then those holy men were so greatly displeased with it? Gregory complains everywhere (book 1, letter 5; likewise letters 7, 25, and so on) that he was distracted beyond measure by outside occupations; that under the guise of the episcopate he had been taken back into the world, being subject to more worldly cares than he remembered ever having had as a layman; that he was so oppressed by the burden of secular affairs as to be unable to raise his mind to the things above; that he was so tossed by the many billows of business, and afflicted by the storms of a tumultuous life, that he might well say, "I have come into the depths of the sea." It is certain that amid these worldly occupations he could still teach the people in sermons, admonish in private, and correct those who needed it; order the Church, give counsel to his colleagues, and exhort them to their duty. Moreover, some time was left for writing; and yet he laments it as his calamity that he was plunged into the very deepest sea. If the administration at that time was a sea, what shall we say of the present Papacy? For what resemblance is there between the two periods? Now there are no sermons, no care for discipline, no zeal for the churches, no spiritual function; nothing, in short, but the world. And yet this labyrinth is praised as if nothing better ordered and arranged could be found. What complaints, too, does Bernard pour out, what groans does he utter, when he beholds the vices of his own age? What then would he have done had he beheld this iron age of ours, or, if possible, an age worse than iron? How dishonest it is, therefore, not only to defend obstinately as sacred and divine what all the saints have always with one voice disapproved, but to abuse their testimony in favor of the Papacy, which, it is evident, was altogether unknown to them! I admit, indeed, regarding the time of Bernard, that all things were then so corrupt as to make it not unlike our own. But it shows a lack of all sense of shame to seek any excuse from that middle period, namely, from that of Leo, Gregory, and the like. For it is just as if someone were to defend the monarchy of the Caesars by praising the ancient state of the Roman empire; in other words, were to borrow the praises of liberty in order to extol tyranny.

Lastly, even if all these things were granted, an entirely new question arises when we deny that there is at Rome a Church in which privileges of this kind can reside, and when we deny that there is a bishop to sustain the dignity of these privileges. Assume, then, that all these things are true (though we have already wrung the contrary from them): that Peter was constituted head of the universal Church by the words of Christ; that he deposited the honor thus conferred on him in the Roman See; that this was sanctioned by the authority of the ancient Church and confirmed by long use; that supreme power was always, by common consent of all, vested in the Roman Pontiff; and that while he was the judge of all causes and all men, he was subject to the judgment of none. Let even more be conceded to them if they wish. I answer in one word, that none of these things avail if there is not a Church and a Bishop at Rome. They must of necessity concede to me that she is not the mother of churches who is not herself a church, and that he cannot be the chief of bishops who is not himself a bishop. Would they, then, have the Apostolic See at Rome? Let them show me a true and lawful apostleship. Would they have a supreme pontiff? Let them show me a bishop. But how? Where will they show me any semblance of a church? They talk of one, no doubt, and have it always on their lips. But surely the Church is recognized by certain marks, and bishopric is the name of an office. I am not now speaking of the people but of the government, which ought to be continually conspicuous in the Church. Where, then, is a ministry such as the institution of Christ requires? Let us remember what was said earlier about the duty of presbyters and bishops. If we bring the office of cardinals to that test, we will acknowledge that they are anything but presbyters. But I should like to know what single quality of a bishop the Pope himself has. The first point in the office of a bishop is to instruct the people in the word of God; the second, and next to it, is to administer the sacraments; the third is to admonish and exhort, to correct those who are at fault, and to restrain the people by holy discipline. Which of these things does he do? Indeed, which of these things does he even pretend to do? Let them say, then, on what ground they would have him regarded as a bishop, who does not, even in appearance, touch any part of the duty with his little finger.

It is not with a bishop as with a king. The latter, though he does not carry out the proper duty of a king, nevertheless retains the title and the honor; but in judging a bishop, regard is had to the command of Christ, which ought always to be given effect in the Church. Let the Romanists, then, untie this knot. I deny that their pontiff is the prince of bishops, since he is no bishop. They must prove this claim of mine false if they would make good their own. What, then, do I maintain? That he has nothing proper to a bishop, but is in all things the opposite of a bishop. But where shall I begin here? With doctrine or with morals? What shall I say, or what shall I pass over in silence, or where shall I end? This I maintain: while in the present day the world is so flooded with perverse and impious doctrines, so full of every kind of superstition, so blinded by error and sunk in idolatry, there is not one of these which has not issued from the Papacy, or at least been confirmed by it. Nor is there any other reason why the pontiffs are so enraged against the reviving doctrine of the Gospel, why they strain every nerve to crush it, and urge all kings and princes to cruelty, than this: that they see their whole dominion tottering and falling to pieces the moment the Gospel of Christ prevails. Leo was cruel, and Clement bloodthirsty; Paul is ferocious. But in attacking the truth, it is not so much natural temper that drives them as the conviction that they have no other way of maintaining their power. Therefore, since they cannot be safe unless they put Christ to flight, they labor in this cause as if they were fighting for their altars and hearths, for their own lives and those of their followers. What then? Shall we recognize the Apostolic See where we see nothing but horrible apostasy? Shall he be the vicar of Christ who, by his furious efforts in persecuting the Gospel, plainly declares himself to be Antichrist? Shall he be the successor of Peter who goes about with fire and sword demolishing everything that Peter built? Shall he be the Head of the Church who, after severing the Church from Christ, her only true Head, tears and mangles her members? Rome, indeed, was once the mother of all the churches; but since she began to be the seat of Antichrist, she has ceased to be what she was.

To some we seem slanderous and insolent when we call the Roman Pontiff Antichrist. But those who think so do not see that they are bringing a charge of intemperance against Paul, after whom we speak, indeed, in whose very words we speak. But lest anyone object that Paul's words have a different meaning, and are twisted by us against the Roman Pontiff, I will briefly show that they can be understood only of the Papacy. Paul says that Antichrist would sit in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). In another passage the Spirit, portraying him in the person of Antiochus, says that his reign would be with great swelling words of vanity (Daniel 7:25). From this we infer that his tyranny is over souls more than over bodies, a tyranny set up in opposition to the spiritual kingdom of Christ. Further, his nature is such that he does not abolish the name either of Christ or of the Church, but rather uses the name of Christ as a pretext, and lurks under the name of the Church as under a mask. But though all the heresies and schisms which have existed from the beginning belong to the kingdom of Antichrist, yet when Paul foretells that the falling away will come, he indicates by this description that that seat of abomination will be set up when a kind of universal falling away comes upon the Church, even though many members of the Church, scattered here and there, should continue in the true unity of the faith. But when he adds that in his own time the mystery of iniquity, which was afterward to be openly revealed, had begun to work in secret, we understand from this that this calamity was neither to be introduced by one man nor to end with one man (see Calvin on 2 Thessalonians 2:3; Daniel 7:9). Moreover, when the mark by which he distinguishes Antichrist is that he would rob God of his honor and take it to himself, he gives the leading feature we ought to follow in searching out Antichrist, especially when pride of this kind proceeds to the open devastation of the Church. Since, then, it is certain that the Roman Pontiff has shamelessly transferred to himself the most distinctive attributes of God and Christ, there can be no doubt that he is the leader and standard-bearer of an impious and abominable kingdom.

Let the Romanists now go and oppose us with antiquity; as if, amid so complete a change in every respect, the honor of the See could continue where there is no See. Eusebius says that God, to make way for his vengeance, transferred the Church which was at Jerusalem to Pella (Eusebius, book 3, chapter 5). What we are told was done once may have been done repeatedly. Hence it is too absurd and ridiculous to tie the honor of the primacy to a particular place in such a way that he who is in fact the most inveterate enemy of Christ, the chief adversary of the Gospel, the greatest destroyer and waster of the Church, the most cruel slayer and murderer of the saints, should nevertheless be regarded as the vicegerent of Christ, the successor of Peter, and the first priest of the Church, merely because he occupies what was formerly the first of all sees. I do not say how great the difference is between the chancery of the Pope and well-regulated order in the Church, although this one fact might well settle the question. For no man of sound mind will locate the episcopate in lead and bulls, much less in that administration of tricks and snares in which the spiritual government of the Pope is supposed to consist. It has therefore been aptly said that that vaunted Roman Church was long ago converted into a temporal court, the only thing now seen at Rome. I am not speaking here of the vices of individuals, but demonstrating that the Papacy itself is diametrically opposed to the ecclesiastical order.

But if we come to individuals, it is well known what kind of vicars of Christ we shall find. No doubt Julius and Leo, Clement and Paul, will be pillars of the Christian faith and the foremost interpreters of religion, though they knew nothing more of Christ than they had learned in the school of Lucian. But why name three or four pontiffs? As if there were any doubt about the kind of religion professed by the pontiffs, with their College of Cardinals and their professors, at the present day. The first article of the secret theology in vogue among them is that there is no God. Another is that whatever has been written and is taught concerning Christ is lies and imposture. Erasmus, in a letter to Steuchus, says: "It may be that in Germany there are persons who do not refrain from blasphemy against God, but the severest punishment is inflicted on them. But at Rome I have heard with my own ears men belching out horrid blasphemies against Christ and his apostles, in the presence of many besides myself, and doing it with impunity!"

But let us suppose that the wickedness of these pontiffs whom I have mentioned is not known, since they have not published it in sermons or writings, but betrayed it only at table or in their chamber, or at least within the walls of their court. But if they would have the privilege they claim confirmed, they must strike from their list of pontiffs John XXII. John Gerson, who lived at the time, attests that John XXII openly denied the immortality of the soul.

But I take no pleasure in this absurd mode of disputation, and therefore return to the point from which I digressed. To tie Christ and the Holy Spirit and the Church to a particular place, so that everyone who presides there, even if he were a devil, must still be considered the vicegerent of Christ and the head of the Church, because that place was formerly the See of Peter, is not only impious and insulting to Christ, but absurd and contrary to common sense. For a long time the Roman pontiffs have either been altogether devoid of religion or been its greatest enemies. The see which they occupy, therefore, no more makes them the vicars of Christ than it makes an idol become God when it is placed in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). Then, if their conduct is examined, let the popes answer for themselves what there is in them that could make them be recognized as bishops. First, the manner of life at Rome, at which they not only wink and keep silent but also tacitly approve, is altogether unworthy of bishops, whose duty it is to curb the license of the people by the strictness of discipline. But I will not be so severe with them as to charge them with the faults of others. But when they, with their household, with almost the whole College of Cardinals, and the whole body of their clergy, are so given over to wickedness, obscenity, uncleanness, iniquity, and crime of every kind that they resemble monsters more than men, they thereby betray that they are anything but bishops. They need not fear that I will expose their vileness further. For it is painful to wade through such filthy mire, and I must spare modest ears. But I think I have amply demonstrated what I set out to show, namely, that though Rome was formerly the first of churches, she does not deserve at the present day to be regarded as one of her least members.

As for those whom they call cardinals, I do not know how it happened that they rose so suddenly to such a height. In the age of Gregory, the name was applied to bishops only (Gregory, book 2, letters 15, 77, 79; letters 6, 25). For whenever he mentions cardinals, he assigns them not only to the Roman Church but to every other church, so that, in short, a cardinal priest is nothing else than a bishop. I do not find the name among the writers of an earlier age. I see, however, that they were inferior to bishops, whom they now far surpass. There is a well-known passage in Augustine: "Although, according to the titles of honor which custom has established in the Church, the office of bishop is greater than that of presbyter, yet in many things Augustine is inferior to Jerome" (Augustine to Jerome, Letter 19). Here, certainly, he is not distinguishing a presbyter of the Roman Church from other presbyters, but placing all of them alike after bishops. And this was so strictly observed that at the Council of Carthage, when two legates of the Roman See were present, one a bishop and the other a presbyter, the latter was put in the lowest place. But not to dwell too much on ancient times, we have an account of a council held at Rome under Gregory, at which the presbyters sit in the lowest place and sign by themselves, while the deacons do not sign at all. And indeed they had no office at that time except to be present under the bishop and assist him in the administration of the word and sacraments. So greatly is their lot now changed that they have become the companions of kings and Caesars. And there can be no doubt that they have grown gradually along with their head, until they reached their present pinnacle of dignity. This much it seemed proper to say in passing, so that my readers may understand how very widely the Roman See as it now exists differs from the ancient See, under which it tries to cloak and defend itself. But whatever they were formerly, since they have no true and lawful office in the Church, they retain only a color and an empty mask. Indeed, since they are in every respect the opposite of true ministers, what Gregory so often writes must of necessity have befallen them. His words are: "Weeping I say it, groaning I declare it: when the priestly order has fallen within, it cannot long stand without" (Gregory, book 4, letters 55, 56; book 5, letter 7). Or rather, what Malachi says of such persons must be fulfilled in them: "You are departed out of the way; you have caused many to stumble at the law; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi, saith the Lord of hosts. Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people" (Malachi 2:8, 9). I now leave all the godly to judge what the supreme pinnacle of the Roman hierarchy must be, to which the Papists, with wicked effrontery, do not hesitate to subject even the word of God itself, that word which ought to be revered and holy in earth and heaven, by men and angels.
